Wind Up and Wound Down by Goveri-999

[pagebreak]

It is a matter of some misconception when people refer to those unfortunate automata existing in the crypts as 'undead', while they are nothing of the sort. They are not, in fact, even dead. Their mechanics still function normally. They are perfectly, and even preternaturally, healthy. However, they lack the breath of God that infuses us all; they have no pneuma, and are soulless husks, half-mer bound to this world. The Rewound. Unwinding is a rather natural, though euphemistic, phrase that means the death of the body and the passing of the soul to the Dreaming Sleeve and the collective well of souls from which all spring. Through some accident or errant twitch of fate, the mechanisms powering our bodies can, on rare occasion, begin operating again even after the pneuma has faded. They retain access to some flickering memories, here and there, and are even capable of some level of thought, but largely merely attempt to follow through with whatever the fabricant was doing when he died, over and over again, stuck in a loop, and if jarred from this loop will become hostile and enraged. At this point, it is tempting to attempt to destroy the body and move on. However, it is not so simple to do so. The rewinding process gives their bodies a massive surge of power, without will or soul to restrain it, and even if attacked will shrug off immediately fatal wounds and heal absurdly quickly. The only way to defeat them is to unwind them once again, to slow their mechanisms and stop them completely. Merely paralyzing them is ineffective, as it is a temporary and essentially illusory suspension of function rather than an actual degradation of the corpus. Only when they stop moving will they shut down for a second and final time.

[This is a collection of mutterings of the High Foremer, as recorded by his scribe Alammu 73912]

[pagebreak]

Power. Energy. Materiality in potentia, daedronics, however you want to describe it. That which allows motion, the agent of change. Only made possible by the intermingling of Anu and Padomay, Change and Stasis, IS and IS NOT. Exists infinitely but unusable in Aetherius, spiralling constantly towards entropy in Oblivion. All that is in the Grey Maybe requires some form of it, and the sources are myriad. Magnus. AnuLorkhan. Mundane kinesis. It requires power to move power. The further away something is from the source, the harder it is to move power there and the more you lose along the way. It's slippery. Always jumping. Always wants to escape. Except dracochrysalids, but those require more power to produce than you can possibly get and aren't very useful anyways. Religious experiment. Idiot Saliache keep trying. When building infrastructure, build close to power. Less waste. Efficient. Great construction requires enormous power. And if the power dies, the closest and the greatest are the first and worst affected. Fundamental axiom. In magic, in politics, in theosophy. No-one seems to notice. No-one seems to learn.

De Rerum Mutabilitatis By Quintus Sextus Septus VIII

[pagebreak]

I write this treatise in honor and mourning of the death of the last known Mimic, hacked to pieces by an irate adventurer who found that the door he was opening led to a closet filled with gnashing teeth rather than the handful of Septims he was presumably expecting. It is a great blow to the academic community, given that mimics were unique in their ability to shift forms at will and their willingness to remain stationary for extended periods. Created by a mad Chimeri wizard some time in the first two centuries of the First Era, mimics were designed to be the perfect guardians of the treasure troves that old mages inevitably seem to collect. However, they were an odd blend of flesh and metal the likes of which Nirn had never before seen, nor would ever see again. Because of their artificial creation, there was a finite number of them, though over the centuries they disseminated throughout northern Tamriel, ranging from Morrowind to High Rock. They would typically find for themselves a disused room and take on a form alluring to people rummaging about, blending well with the surrounding environs. They did not actually require sustenance, but seemed to relish feasting on the unwary regardless, most probably because their creator had a twisted sense of humor.

How Two Moon By Andy

[pagebreak]

...I hypothesize, based on de-encoded Dreamsleeve memospores intended for the thrice-forsaken House Wizards of the varliance-rend, that, with high probability, it may be possible to re-enact the traumatic birth of this world without, as it were, the trauma. By reversing the failure of the C-signs, Pigmius in particular, through use not of padhomaic nor draconid-wrought thaumaturgy, but rather through the metals and machinations of Our Lord, we avoid the drama caused by personality and the violence of self. We avoid both the Scarab and the Scarab-framer, don't you see? They intended it to the thus! They were created, they create, and we created them in return! And now we create anew a perfect clockwork world, drifting through Oblivion, unmarred by fleshy imperfection....

Chronography, Volume 1 By Monden Marvayn

[pagebreak]

Knowledge and the knowledge of that knowledge comes and goes. What one generation knows for a fact the next only knows as myth. Such is not the case with the Skyriders, better known to me and my fellow Dunmer scholars as the Pearlescent Chronographers. While those not from Morrowind may not recognize the name, natives will no doubt at this point be familiar with who I speak of. To the uninitiated, I say welcome, and let me answer both yours and my fellow kinsmen lingering questions on the mysterious clockwork gift-givers. History: What we first knew of the Chronographers came from our encounters with them. Or perhaps Encounters, for the shows they so performed no doubt deserve a capital letter. And while incredible, mind-shattering, and all-around unusual, the Chronographers always behaved the same in a situation. Dunmer, in their time of need, would find fleets of whirling dwemer contraptions, or mechanical creatures descending from the sky, upon which rode mystics, dressed in metal, with fire-red eyes and limbs of steel. These visitors would impart upon the needy contraptions and physical riddles, which in time would reveal their purpose, always benevolent and helpful. It was only after careful studying, and a chance meeting an interview with one of these Chronographers, that we learned the truth. The Chronographers Pious dunmer may know of the Mystery of Morrowind, otherwise known as Sotha Sil, Seht, or the Clockwork King. A mystic, an engineer, and former god of the Dunmer people, Sotha Sil retreated into his mysterious Clockwork City many years ago, where he was killed by his friend and fellow Tribunal member, Almalexia. What many do not know however, is what happened following this. You see, his city was not merely a workshop, but a sprawling metropolis. And in this metropolis live fabricants, mer-machines, living automatons who worked and loved in the city. But with their king and creator dead, the fabricants were faced with a decision. Stay in their home, no doubt soon to crumble without its creator to guide it, or leave? While a schism may have divided other such people, the fabricants were unanimously swayed by a group known as the Armour of Oscillating Quartz (see volume 3: origins). This group swayed the city into following them aboard a fleet of mysterious "helicarriers" (see volume 2: technology) from which they sailed out of the city, no doubt seeking a new purpose in their lives, for what are machines without purpose?
